newsitem.title: HAITI: Human rights report on Haiti sees more violence.
newsitem.headline: Human rights report on Haiti sees more violence.

text.p: Almost two years after 20,000 U.S.-led troops restored Haiti's first freely-elected president, a leading human rights group said on Thursday that the U.S. and Haitian governments have not done enough to uphold human rights in the Caribbean nation.

Haiti could backslide into violence and repression once U.N. peacekeepers leave unless the U.S. and Haitian governments act to bring human rights violators to justice, Washington-based Human Rights Watch/Americas said in a report.
"In this story, the United States does not come out with its hands clean," said Sarah DeCosse, an attorney and research associate with the rights group who co-authored the report.

Human Rights Watch charges the U.S. government with obstructing justice by refusing to return documents seized by U.S. troops from the headquarters of a right-wing paramilitary group, the Haitian Front for Advancement and Progress (FRAPH).

FRAPH was blamed for a host of rights abuses during the three-year military dictatorship that followed the September 1991 coup that ousted President Jean-Bertrand Aristide, Haiti's first freely elected leader.
The National Coalition for Haitian Rights estimates that 5,000 Haitians were murdered during those three years.

U.S. troops that restored Aristide on Oct. 15, 1994, seized some 160,000 pages from FRAPH headquarters. Those documents are believed to include information about the FRAPH chain of command and activities, as well as photos of torture and murder victims.
The report criticised the United States for refusing to return the documents, which are potentially valuable evidence in human rights abuse cases.

U.S. embassy officials have said they would return the FRAPH documents as long as the names of U.S. citizens were deleted to protect their privacy, but that Haiti has not agreed to do that. They also denied the documents contain information that would help prosecute human rights abuses.

Human Rights Watch also condemned a secret deal made by the U.S. government to allow Emmanuel Constant, the head of the now defunct FRAPH, to remain at his mother's house in New York, despite an extradition request by Haitian authorities.
"It is truly appalling, considering the role Constant played in FRAPH, that they would offer him this kind of deal," said DeCosse.

The rights groups called on the United States to return the FRAPH documents, extradite Constant and review allegations of CIA, U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration and Defence Intelligence Agency involvement in human rights abuses.
Constant would face murder and other charges in Haiti if his extradition were granted. He has repeatedly stated that he was paid by the CIA while operating in Haiti.
A spokeswoman for the U.S. embassy in Port-au-Prince on Thursday declined comment on the return of Constant and allegations of CIA involvement in Haitian human rights abuses.
